_note: Which of several same-named people in the tree a register record belongs to.
register.json keys record rows by the NAME on the document, because that is all a
document gives. Eight names are carried by more than one person in this tree, and
until 20 September 2026 their records were shown on every candidate's page under
'filed under the name, not assigned to this person'. Honest, and not an answer.
Seven of the eight separate on a date. Each rule below names a distinguishing
string from the record's own text and the slug it belongs to. 'default' catches
the rest of that name's records. A slug of null means the record belongs to NONE
of the tree people of that name — which happened once, and mattered.
Rules are matched case-insensitively against the record's `says` text, FIRST MATCH
WINS, so order matters. A rule that never fires is a failure and not a no-op:
check_links.py refuses it. That caught two redundant rules here on the first run —
both were unreachable behind '3 JULY 1808', which had already claimed the same

thomas saniger._why: THREE men, not two. The tree holds the 1711 and the 1744. Four of the eight records belong to a third Thomas — baptised Berkeley 3 July 1808, son of John, Hannah's brother — who is NOT in the family tree at all and is written about at /thomas-sinegar/. Attaching his life to either tree Thomas would have merged two men born ninety-seven years apart.

george pitt d'arcy._why: The major of the 39th Foot, 1783-1849, and his grandson the railway clerk, 1864-1931. Everything military is the major's; the Queensland death registration is the clerk's.

catherine d'arcy._why: All six records are one woman at Brighton between 1841 and 1876, aged 86 at death and born Barbadoes — which is the 1789 Catherine. The 1867 Catherine was born in Brisbane and outlived all of it.

constantine d'arcy._why: All six belong to the younger man: christened St Michael, Barbados, February 1786, commissioned 1804 and 1805, dead at Chatham in May 1805. The elder Constantine died in 1778, before the earliest of them.

samuel charles sneyd._why: The gaol governor, baptised Hanley 1811 and dead in Queensland in 1885. His grandson of the same name was born in 1863 and has none of these.

james sneyd._why: Both records are the Hanley engraver of Well Street — aged 33 in one and 53 in 1871 in the other, so born about 1818. The Madeley James of 1779 is a different man.

mary sneyd._why: Baptised Hanley in February 1814 to Samuel and Elizabeth, sister to Samuel Charles. Not the Madeley Mary of 1788.

william sneyd._why: NOT SETTLED, and deliberately left so. Four men of this name are in the tree and the records will not separate cleanly: the weaver who married Mary Blackbourne at Madeley in 1769 has a baptism of 1742 in the record and a birth of 1746 in the tree, and the two burials — 1819 aged 88 and 1827 aged 84 — give births of about 1731 and about 1743, so at most one of them can be his. Choosing here would be inventing a man. These stay filed under the name until the Madeley register settles them.
